blocks.text: Adapter tuning inserts small additional neural network layers, called adapters, directly into an existing pretrained model architecture, training only those newly inserted layers while every original weight in the model stays completely frozen.

Adapters were among the earliest widely adopted PEFT methods, and understanding their bottleneck structure and insertion pattern makes the more recent methods covered elsewhere in this module, LoRA especially, easier to appreciate by comparison.

An adapter is a small additional block of layers spliced directly into the existing network, positioned so the original data flow passes through it, letting it learn a task specific transformation on top of the frozen model existing computation.

In a typical transformer layer, adapters are commonly inserted after the attention sublayer and after the feed-forward sublayer, both covered in the Foundation Models module, positions chosen because they sit at natural points in the existing computation where a small learned adjustment can meaningfully influence downstream behavior.
3. The Bottleneck Structure of an Adapter

blocks.alt: The Bottleneck Structure of an Adapter

blocks.text: An adapter typically follows a bottleneck shape, a down projection layer that shrinks the representation to a much smaller dimension, followed by an up projection layer that expands it back to the original size, keeping the total number of new parameters small even though the adapter touches a high dimensional representation.

During training, gradients flow through the adapter parameters and get applied to update them, while the base model original weights, positioned before and after the adapter in the data flow, remain completely frozen throughout, exactly the PEFT pattern introduced in the What Is PEFT topic earlier in this module.

At inference, the trained adapter stays inserted in the network, its output added into the ongoing computation exactly where it was placed during training, meaning the deployed model runs both the frozen base weights and the adapter together as one combined forward pass.

Because the base model stays frozen and unchanged, several different adapters can be trained independently for different tasks, all sharing the same underlying base model, swapped in or out depending on which task is being handled at any given moment.

blocks.title: This connects directly to the Adapter Fusion topic later in this module
blocks.content: When several adapters need to work together rather than being swapped independently, adapter fusion, covered as its own topic, provides a way to learn how to combine them.

blocks.text: Adapter tuning trains a small fraction of the total parameter count compared to full fine-tuning, delivering the familiar PEFT tradeoff, dramatically lower memory and storage cost in exchange for a somewhat smaller pool of trainable capacity.

blocks.text: Inserting adapter layers directly into the model computation path adds a small amount of inference latency, since the forward pass now runs through extra layers it would not otherwise pass through, a consideration that later PEFT methods like LoRA were partly designed to address by allowing the trained parameters to be merged back into the base weights rather than staying as a separate inserted block.
9. Adapter Tuning's Place in PEFT History

Adapter tuning helped establish the core PEFT idea, freeze the base, train a small addition, that every method covered later in this module builds on in one form or another, even though more recent methods like LoRA have become more commonly used in practice for many fine-tuning projects today.
A team wants to fine-tune a shared base model for three different internal tools, a code reviewer, a documentation writer, and a bug triager, without maintaining three separate full model copies.

They insert and train a separate small adapter for each tool, keeping the base model frozen and shared across all three, swapping in the relevant adapter depending on which tool a request is routed to, achieving three specialized behaviors from one shared underlying model.

items: Forgetting to freeze the base model weights, accidentally training the entire network instead of just the adapter
Choosing an adapter bottleneck dimension so small it cannot capture the needed task specific adjustment
Ignoring the inference latency added by extra adapter layers when evaluating deployment cost
Assuming adapters and LoRA are interchangeable without understanding their different insertion and merging behavior

Adapter tuning inserts small bottleneck shaped layers directly into a frozen pretrained model, training only those inserted layers, and while it adds a small amount of inference overhead compared to methods that can merge back into the base weights, it established the foundational PEFT pattern that later methods like LoRA build directly on.
